rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqmān’s warning against associating partners and the divine charge to honor parents jointly guard against two gravest sins.
rows.anchor: combined with the “charge”given to human beings about parents constitute protection against the two

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet identifies associating partners with God and disrespecting parents among the greatest major sins.
rows.anchor: the Prophet asked his Companions, “Shall I tell you what are the greatest of major sins? . . . To attribute partners to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Goodness, gratitude, and virtue toward parents are enjoined elsewhere, often alongside worshipping God alone.
rows.anchor: Goodness, gratitude, and virtue toward parents are enjoined in several verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to be virtuous toward parents is the first injunction of the covenant in 2:83.
rows.anchor: In 2:83, Be virtuous toward parents is listed as the first injunction of the covenant

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭs
rows.claim: “Weakness upon weakness” refers to the hardships of childbearing.
rows.anchor: Weakness upon weakness refers to the hardships of childbearing (IK, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir’s abbreviated citation also allows “weakness upon weakness” to mean exhaustion upon exhaustion.
rows.anchor: can also mean “exhaustion upon exhaustion” (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two-year weaning period indicates that full two-year breastfeeding is best when possible.
rows.anchor: it is best for a child to be breast-fed for a full two years when possible

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving thanks to God is through praise and obedience; gratitude to parents is shown through righteousness and maintaining kinship ties.
rows.anchor: Giving thanks unto God is said to be accomplished through praise and obedience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Enjoining right and forbidding wrong is a major Quranic ethical injunction.
rows.anchor: To enjoin right and forbid wrong is a major ethical injunction of the Quran

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: In context, after people perfect their own worship, they can help others perfect theirs through enjoining right and forbidding wrong.
rows.anchor: then they can help others perfect theirs (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The translated phrase presents this as a course humans must resolve to follow.
rows.anchor: indicates that the phrase relates to the importance of human beings resolving to follow such a course

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭūsī offers an alternative: it is among matters God has resolved, determined, or commanded.
rows.anchor: it can also be understood to mean that it is a course or matter that God has resolved, determined, or commanded (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aḥzāb is a Madinan sūrah believed to have followed Āl ʿImrān immediately.
rows.anchor: A Madinan sūrah, al-Aḥzāb is believed to have been revealed immediately after Sūrah 3

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name refers to the confederates, an alliance of Quraysh and other Arab and Jewish tribes who fought the Muslims at the Trench in 5/627.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its name

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The confederates numbered an estimated ten thousand men, six hundred horses, and many camels, against about three thousand Madinans who had six days to prepare.
rows.anchor: The strength of the confederate armies is estimated to have been around ten thousand men with six hundred horses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Salmān al-Fārsī’s advice, defenders dug a trench north of Madinah between natural lava defenses; excavated earth shielded them and supplied rocks, while the trench blocked cavalry.
rows.anchor: They employed a strategy suggested by the Persian Salmān al-Fārsī and heretofore unknown to the Arabs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Southern gardens already impeded an attack by forcing attackers into long, ambush-prone columns, and patrols turned fighting into a month-long siege of small skirmishes.
rows.anchor: These defenses limited the fighting to small skirmishes and turned the battle into a test of wits and wills

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The confederates failed to cross the trench and persuaded Banū Qurayẓah to admit a southern attack, but the Muslims sowed dissension and disrupted talks.
rows.anchor: the Muslims, however, caught wind of this plan and managed to sow dissension between the Quraysh and the Banū Qurayẓah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s offer of one-third of Madinah’s date crop to Banū Ghaṭafān strained the alliance even though treaty terms were never agreed; dissension, low morale, and a sandstorm ended the siege.
rows.anchor: the fact that a large part of the confederacy had entered into negotiations with the Prophet strained the already tense relations within the confederacy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the siege, the Muslims forced Banū Qurayẓah’s unconditional surrender; for treasonous negotiations that broke Madinah’s treaty, the men were sentenced to death and women and children taken captive.
rows.anchor: For their act of treason in negotiating with an opposing force and thus breaking the treaty of Madinah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The defeat cost the Makkans much prestige and was their last major battle with the Muslims before the conquest of Makkah in 8/630.
rows.anchor: was the last major battle between the Muslims and the Quraysh before the conquest of Makkah in 8/630

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah highlights the Prophet’s central status: he is closer to believers than themselves and an exemplary model for those hoping in God and the Last Day.
rows.anchor: al-Aḥzāb is significant for highlighting the importance of the Prophet in Islam and the status of his wives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers are counseled to obey the Prophet, especially when he has decreed a matter; though not their biological father, he is their spiritual father and his wives are their mothers.
rows.anchor: it confirms his status as a spiritual father to all believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah calls the Prophet a witness, warner, bearer of glad tidings, caller to God, Seal of the prophets, and luminous lamp.
rows.anchor: this sūrah refers to him as the Seal of the prophets (v. 40) and a luminous lamp (v. 46)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah celebrates God and the angels blessing the Prophet and commands believers to invoke blessings upon him.
rows.anchor: declares that God and His angels invoke blessings upon the Prophet and enjoins the believers to do so as well

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s wives have a status above other women, while the People of the House are those God desires to purify of defilements.
rows.anchor: the family of the Prophet, here referred to as the People of the House, are said to be those whom God desires to purify

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Love for the Prophet and his family has long been considered foundational to faith, based on these verses and many hadiths.
rows.anchor: love for the Prophet and his family has long been regarded as a foundational component of faith

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A prophetic saying directs people to love God for His blessings, the Prophet for God’s sake, and the Prophet’s household for the Prophet’s sake.
rows.anchor: In the words of the Prophet, “Love God for how He nourishes you from His Blessings. Love me for the love of God. And love the people

rows.speaker: Sufyān al-Thawrī
rows.claim: Sufyān al-Thawrī says that loving whom God loves is loving God, and honoring whom God honors is honoring God.
rows.anchor: Sufyān al-Thawrī(d. 161/778) is reported to have said

none: Surah translation only; no commentary points to record.

rows.speaker: Q, Sy
rows.claim: The Trust is understood as the dictates of faith and belief, as expressed in a famous saying that one without trust has no belief.
rows.anchor: The Trust is understood as relating to the dictates of faith and belief, as in a famous saying

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Many commentators identify the Trust with obedience.
rows.anchor: Many relate the Trust to obedience (IK, Ṭ, Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: IJ, JJ, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Most commentators take the Trust to mean the religious obligations (farāʾiḍ).
rows.anchor: understood by most as a reference to the requirements

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another reported interpretation takes the Trust to refer to prayer alone.
rows.anchor: though others see it as a reference to prayer alone (Q)

rows.speaker: IJ, Q
rows.claim: The Trust can concern management of each faculty, including tongue, eye, stomach, and sexual parts; this view is linked to 8:27.
rows.anchor: The Trust can also be understood as pertaining to the manner in which one manages each aspect of one’s being

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Another view sees the Trust as inner faith and outward performance of religion’s requirements.
rows.anchor: It is also said that the Trust pertains to faith inwardly and performing the requirements of religion outwardly (Aj)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The Trust may be the primordial tawḥīd covenant and testimony to God’s Lordship made with all humanity before earthly life.
rows.anchor: the pact or covenant of tawḥīd (Divine Oneness) and the witness to God’s Lordship made with all of humanity

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators understand the Trust’s offer to the heavens, earth, and mountains literally.
rows.anchor: taken literally by many commentators

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs, Ṭū
rows.claim: Another view says the offer was made to their inhabitants: all people of earth, jinn, and angels.
rows.anchor: offered to their inhabitants (R), that is, to all the people of the earth, the jinn, and the angels (Ṭs, Ṭū)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavens, earth, and mountains refused because they shrank from a burden they knew was too heavy, not from defiance.
rows.anchor: They refused to bear it not out of defiance, but because they shrank from what they knew to be too heavy a burden

rows.speaker: Bḍ, IJ, IK, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Many say they chose passive obedience because accountability entails possible reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: they knew they would be subject to reward and punishment and thus chose to remain passively obedient

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: The heavens, earth, and mountains recognized their weakness, while humans understood their station and accepted responsibility as rational beings fit for religious obligations.
rows.anchor: human beings realized their place and assumed their responsibility (R) as creatures possessing intellect and thus fit to observe the obligations of religion (Z)

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭū
rows.claim: A metaphorical interpretation says that despite their size and grandeur, the heavens, earth, and mountains lack capacity for revealed laws, as 59:21 illustrates.
rows.anchor: as in 59:21: Had We made this Quran descend upon a mountain, thou wouldst have seen it humbled

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity’s unique responsibility is to remain in tawḥīd and follow the practices of its religious laws.
rows.anchor: That man bore it thus indicates the unique responsibility human beings bear to remain in a state of tawḥīd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Breaking that duty breaches humanity’s pre-world covenant with God and violates its true nature.
rows.anchor: they break the covenant they made with God before entering this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Man is an ignorant wrongdoer because he fails to bear the Trust’s full weight.
rows.anchor: Man . . . has proved himself an ignorant wrongdoer insofar as he has failed to bear the full weight of the Trust

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some restrict ignorant wrongdoers to disbelievers and hypocrites, who are ignorant of God, and to tyrants.
rows.anchor: some understand this phrase as a reference only to disbelievers and hypocrites, who are ignorant of God

rows.speaker: M
rows.claim: Another interpretation refers to Adam, who accepted the Trust without realizing its full import.
rows.anchor: others take it as a reference to Adam, meaning that when he accepted the Trust, he did not realize its full import (M)

rows.speaker: Ṭū, Z
rows.claim: Another view applies the phrase to all humans, ignorant of the Trust’s responsibility and wronging themselves through disobedience.
rows.anchor: a reference to all human beings who are ignorant of the responsibility of the Trust and wrong themselves by committing acts of disobedience

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭū
rows.claim: A minority reading takes “bear the Trust” to mean failing to uphold it and thus failing to carry its burden.
rows.anchor: In a minority reading, the expression “bear the Trust” is understood to mean failing to uphold it

rows.speaker: IJ
rows.claim: One report says Cain bore the Trust’s burden by murdering Abel.
rows.anchor: it is said that Cain bore the burden of the Trust for having murdered Abel (IJ)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The good given to those obedient and righteous in this life may mean Paradise.
rows.anchor: Those who are devoutly obedient and perform righteous deeds in this life will receive the gift of Paradise (JJ)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Alternatively, it may mean good in this life, such as health and peace, and in the next.
rows.anchor: or good in this life (such as health and peace) and in the next (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IK, JJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: The vastness of God’s earth implies emigrating away from idolaters and encourages the Prophet’s contemporaneous Muslims to leave Makkah.
rows.anchor: God’s earth is vast implies that one should emigrate away from the company of idolaters

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The “land of God” may refer to the Garden, which one should seek through righteous deeds.
rows.anchor: the “land of God” in the Garden, which one should seek by performing righteous deeds (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The patient in this verse contrast with those who waver in verse 8.
rows.anchor: those who are patient contrasts with those who waver in v. 8

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: “Without reckoning” means they will not undergo the weighing of deeds in the Judgment balance.
rows.anchor: Without reckoning refers to their not having to endure the weighing of their deeds in the balance on the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fuṣṣilat is a Makkan sūrah believed to follow Ghāfir immediately; its name comes from the Quran’s signs being expounded in verse 3.
rows.anchor: Fuṣṣilat is a Makkan sūrah believed to have been revealed directly after the preceding sūrah, Ghāfir

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: The sūrah is also called Sajdah and ḥā Mīm Sajdah; a less common name, “The Lamps,” comes from verse 12.
rows.anchor: Other less common names for this sūrah are

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Another less common name, “Means of Sustenance,” derives from God’s apportioning earthly provision in verse 10.
rows.anchor: from the reference to God having apportioned means of sustenance

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Some see continuity with Ghāfir in the warnings of punishment for ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Quraysh, echoing 40:82’s lesson from earlier peoples.
rows.anchor: that which they used to earn availed them not (Āl)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Verse 2 can warn Quraysh in a way that echoes 40:83: they mocked the Quran, as verse 26 describes.
rows.anchor: v. 2 can be seen as a warning to the Quraysh that echoes 40:83

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening moves from the Quran’s nature (1–4) to the Prophet’s advice about rejecters (5–6), then contrasts disbelievers and believers (7–8) before creation (9–12).
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with a brief discussion of the nature of the Quran (vv. 1–4)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah recounts the destruction of ʿĀd and Thamūd (13–18), warns of the Hereafter (19–25), then treats rejecters of the Quran (26–28).
rows.anchor: the calamities that befell the pre-Islamic Arabian tribes of ʿĀd and Thamūd as examples of the fate that awaits disbelievers in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers and disbelievers are juxtaposed in 29–32, followed by exhortation to respectful conduct even with disbelievers (33–39), then discussion of the Quran and its rejecters (40–46).
rows.anchor: an exhortation to the believers to maintain respectful speech and conduct even with the disbelievers (vv. 33–39)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section (47–54) reflects on human vicissitudes and how God reveals truth to people, especially in verse 53.
rows.anchor: The final section (vv. 47–54), which reflects upon the vagaries of the human condition

none: Surah translation only; no commentary points to record.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command echoes 23:96, with 29:46 also relevant, and “better” can mean more beautiful or virtuous.
rows.anchor: Better can also mean “more beautiful” or “more virtuous.”

rows.speaker: IJ
rows.claim: Because “repel” has no stated object, one interpretation is to answer anger with patience.
rows.anchor: people should repel anger with patience (IJ)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Another interpretation is to answer error with truth.
rows.anchor: error with truth (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Another interpretation is to answer ignorance with clemency.
rows.anchor: ignorance with clemency (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Another interpretation is to answer wrongdoing with pardon.
rows.anchor: the commission of evil with pardon (IJ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: If others disobey God in their treatment of someone, that person should obey God in responding to them.
rows.anchor: if others disobey God in how they treat an individual, then that person should obey God in how he or she treats them (IK)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Such conduct can produce reconciliation, love, and empathy.
rows.anchor: Such conduct can lead to reconciliation, love, and empathy (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repaying evil with good does not require surrendering to an enemy or accepting falsehood; avoid returning harm when doing so will not cause greater harm.
rows.anchor: avoid reciprocating harm whenever such avoidance will not lead to greater evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith treated as a foundational Islamic principle says there should be neither harm nor reciprocal harm.
rows.anchor: a ḥadīth taken by many as a foundational principle of Islam states, “Let there be no harming and no reciprocating harm.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another hadith commends maintaining ties with those who sever them, giving to those who deny, and overlooking oppressors.
rows.anchor: Another states, “Keep relations with those who cut them off with you, give to those who deny you, and ignore those who oppress you.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command can also apply inwardly: repel one’s own base impulses toward vice by practicing virtue.
rows.anchor: one should repel one’s own base tendencies toward vice by practicing virtue

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Only those who restrain anger and patiently bear harm can repel evil with good.
rows.anchor: those who conceal their anger and bear what harm is done to them with patience (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IJ
rows.claim: A great share may refer to a person’s good fortune.
rows.anchor: A great share refers to one of good fortune (IJ)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: A great share may mean abundant intellect and vision.
rows.anchor: an abundance of intellect and vision (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: A great share may mean elevated virtue, spiritual strength, and inner purity.
rows.anchor: a high degree of virtue, spiritual strength, and inner purity (R)

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: A great share may refer to Paradise.
rows.anchor: Great fortune may also be understood as a reference to Paradise (IJ, Ṭ, Ṭs)
